candidates.statement: It is important to note that for a NAM to be considered for review in drug development, the test 34 does not necessarily need to be validated. However, as FDA gains confidence in these tools, they 35 could be formally adopted to reduce or replace specific animal tests. A fit-for-purpose NAM, 36 even if not validated, may adequately address specific toxicological concerns. When a NAM is 37 used it is always in the context of the weight of evidence (WOE) or, in other words, considering 38 the specific concerns about that product based on prior knowledge and any preclinical 39 toxicological information provided. 40

candidates.statement: Under the regulations governing investigational new drug applications, drug sponsors must 56 submit nonclinical data regarding their proposed product’s pharmacology and toxicology before 57 the proposed product can proceed to clinical trials. 7 This requirement helps FDA minimize risk 58 and determine whether investigational drugs are reasonably safe to proceed in humans. These 59 pharmacology and toxicology data may come from a range of methods, such as in vitro testing, 60 in silico modeling, or combinations thereof. In this guidance, FDA intends to facilitate broader 61 integration of NAMs in drug development and regulatory submission packages. Although 62 animal toxicity studies have previously been relied upon to assess for potential risks to human 63 health from drug products, the development and use of reliable NAMs furthers an important 64 FDA priority to reduce and replace animal testing while advancing predictive toxicology using 65 human-centric methods. 66

NAMs hold great potential in terms of enhancing efficiencies in drug development and 68 generating data to advance human health. For example, NAMs may offer additional tools for 69 identifying potential drug toxicities or mechanisms of action for which there are currently no 70 adequate models, and NAMs that incorporate human biology may provide more predictive and 71 human-relevant information than traditional methods. Therefore, CDER encourages the use of 72 NAMs in regulatory submissions, 8 especially when they improve the predictivity, reliability, and 73 human relevance of nonclinical tests and therefore enhance the safety of subsequent clinical 74 trials. Where nonanimal methods have been shown to accurately characterize the relevant risk, 75 FDA encourages moving to scientifically validated nonanimal methods. CDER also encourages 76 sponsors to consult with the applicable review division if there is uncertainty about the suitability 77 of the method for regulatory use when considering use of a nonanimal testing method believed to 78 be suitable, adequate, and feasible for a proposed regulatory use. We anticipate that early 79 engagement will focus on indication-, disease-, organ-, and endpoint-specific considerations that 80 should include interactions with review divisions. A variety of different types of NAMs data can 81 be included as part of nonclinical submissions; this guidance provides general considerations 82 regarding validation principles that are broadly applicable to all NAMs. 83
candidates.context: Although federal laws and regulations do not stipulate exactly which nonclinical tests sponsors 85 must conduct nor in what model, 9 a common set of studies (e.g., general toxicology, primary 86 pharmacology, and safety pharmacology) is generally conducted before clinical trials in humans 87 are initiated. As a drug development program continues, other nonclinical tests may be needed 88 to support clinical trials (e.g., carcinogenicity studies, developmental and reproductive toxicity 89 studies). These studies can be done in a variety of models, and they provide insight regarding 90 several key issues in drug development, such as mechanism of action, safe starting and 91 maximum tolerated doses. 92

candidates.statement: While many of these investigational new drug-enabling studies have traditionally been 94 conducted in animals, CDER routinely receives and reviews data from studies using NAMs. For 95 NAM data to be useful for regulatory decision-making, however, the data must be reliable and 96 there must be confidence in the methodology used. This confidence is typically obtained 97 through scientific consensus generated by the application of validation criteria to the design, 98 performance, and interpretation of the studies. 99

candidates.statement: Regardless of whether a NAM is qualified, its validation is warranted to help determine the 111 quality of the data produced and how the results should be interpreted for regulatory decision- 112 making. Sponsors should take into account the validation considerations described in this 113 guidance to ensure a given NAM is fit-for-purpose. The Organisation for Economic Co- 114 operation and Development (OECD) test guidelines include additional validated methods that 115 CDER has recognized as acceptable in lieu of in vivo studies in the past. For example, certain 116 NAMs that evaluate eye irritation, skin irritation, and skin sensitization have been accepted as 117 fit-for-purpose. CDER has also accepted NAMs using in vitro reconstructed human epidermis 118 assays to predict risk for human skin sensitization to replace the use of animals (e.g., mice in the 119 local lymph node assay). candidates.context: We note that this guidance focuses solely on considerations for the validation of NAMs and does 101 not address qualification of drug development tools (including NAMs), which is addressed in 102 other guidance. 10 Validation is a process by which the accuracy, reliability, and relevance of a 103 procedure are established for a specific context of use (COU). 11 Qualification is a determination 104 that a drug development tool and its proposed COU can be relied upon to have a specific 105 interpretation and application in drug development and regulatory review. 12 While qualification 106 is useful, validation is critical to establishing the reliability of NAM data for specific situations. 107 CDER will review data from both qualified and validated NAMs used in a drug development 108 program to determine whether its use is appropriate in the particular context. 109 10 See the guidance for

candidates.statement: The COU should clearly define the intended use and regulatory purpose of the NAM to address a 136 specific drug development decision context. An adequate COU will address a data gap and 137 fulfill one or more drug development objectives. For a COU to be useful, it has to answer a 138 scientific and/or drug development question allowing CDER to use that information to support a 139 regulatory decision. The following are examples of COUs that can support regulatory decision- 140 making: (1) supporting the extent of patient monitoring in clinical trials, (2) supporting dosage 141 selection (whether it is first in human or whether it is for later phases of development and 142 chronic use), (3) addressing a mechanistic understanding of an adverse event seen in animals 143 and/or humans (such as identifying off-target effects or exaggerated pharmacology), (4) 144 justifying not using an animal species because it does not add value to regulatory decision- 145 making, and (5) helping to support a WoE approach and predicting risks typically not measured 146 in humans. 147
